job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Jamal Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now, in your job hunt, your first job or your studies.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior developer at a mid-sized insurance company in Leicester. I started in June, so about five months. I maintain an old claims system written in a language most of my friends have never heard of, and I fix small bugs and write reports. I studied computer science at a university in the Midlands, passed with an average mark, and my only work experience was a summer job in a supermarket. I rent a room with two housemates, and my mum cooks for me on Sundays, which saves me a lot. I use an AI coding helper sometimes, mainly when I'm stuck, but my team lead Nadia wants us to check everything it gives us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a relief, because I've seen enough hype. At work I'd tell Nadia the helper is useful for small things and that's it. To friends I'd say it's like every new tool, handy for some and annoying for others. Online I'd say people shouldn't panic, and shouldn't be fooled by promises either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my life is pretty much the same either way. The old claims system will need people for years, so I'm not afraid of losing the job. What I'm afraid of is the money. I owe a big loan, I've got two weeks of rent saved, and pay rises at the insurer come once a year at best. And there aren't many other tech jobs in Leicester if this one goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and try to become really good at the claims system, because nobody else wants to learn it. I'd put £50 a month into savings. I'd keep using the helper now and then, and I'd learn a modern language in the evenings, so I'm not stuck in the old one. I'd look at moving to Birmingham in a couple of years for better pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels fine. A bit grey, but okay. I'd say the money stress is steady and doesn't change my mood much any more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody else wants to learn the old system. Is that an advantage or a trap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, to be honest. It makes me hard to replace, because only two of us understand it. But the skill isn't worth anything outside this company, so it ties me here. Nadia told me that herself, kindly. I'd like to be the person who knows it and also knows something modern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the move to Birmingham change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About £4,000 more a year, I think, and many more tech jobs. But rent is higher, and I'd lose my mum's Sunday dinners, which are worth about £60 a month to me. I'd only go if I had a job offer first. I'm not a big risk-taker.

say: I'd say it's a **relief**, and people shouldn't panic or be fooled by promises.
I'd tell Nadia (my team lead) the helper is useful for **small things**.
think: The old claims system needs people for years, so my **job** feels safe.
My real fear is **money**: a big loan and two weeks of rent saved.
do: Become the expert on the **claims system** nobody else wants to learn.
Put **£50** a month into savings and learn a modern language in the evenings.
Look at moving to **Birmingham** in a couple of years.
feel: A bit grey but okay, with **steady** money stress.
S0.quote: The skill isn't worth anything outside this company, so it ties me here.
fieldNote: His job feels **safe** but his skills are narrow, a trap he describes without drama.
He weighs Birmingham carefully and will only move with an offer.

steps.text: Learn the old claims system until I can fix any fault alone
Put £50 a month into a savings account
Learn a modern programming language in the evenings
Apply to Birmingham firms once I have a year's experience

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's the picture I think is most likely, and it'll be bumpy. At work I'd tell Nadia we should spend time learning where the AI helper fails, so we can use it well. To friends I'd say expect changes in tech first, then everything else. Online I'd say governments should help people retrain, and not leave it to employers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, this is the one that makes me nervous. Writing code and fixing bugs is the main thing these tools do well. At the insurer they've already stopped advertising for one junior role. If the tools get better, they need fewer people like me. But my job is the old system, which the tools handle badly, so I may have more time than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI helper every day and work out where it saves time. I'd take a cloud or testing qualification, something that proves I can check and manage the machine's output. I'd make myself useful to the claims team by learning their rules, because that knowledge isn't in code. I'd also cut my spending more and save £100 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels uncomfortable, like when the train's slowing and you aren't sure if it's your station. I'd say mostly worried, but still looking for the exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the insurer stopped advertising one junior role. How did you find out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lad on the desk next to me, Callum (a fellow junior developer), told me the job ad disappeared the week after a tool demo. Nobody said anything officially. It could be a coincidence, but I don't think so. Since then I've been checking the vacancies page every Monday, which isn't healthy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use the claims team's rules to protect your place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit with the claims handlers one afternoon a week and learn how they decide what's covered. That's the knowledge the tools don't have yet, and it's what the firm can't easily replace. If I can say, I know the code and I know the claims, I'm a more difficult person to cut.

say: I'd tell Nadia (my team lead) to learn where the AI helper **fails**.
I'd say governments should help people **retrain**, not leave it to employers.
think: Writing code and fixing bugs is what these tools do **well**, and my firm already stopped hiring a junior.
The old system is badly handled by tools, so I may have more **time**.
do: Use the AI helper **daily** and learn where it saves time.

Steady style shows in measured, specific steps.

steps.text: Use the AI helper daily and note where it gets claims code wrong
Take a testing qualification in the evenings
Sit with the claims handlers every Thursday afternoon
Save £100 a month by cutting takeaways and trips

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's too fast for anyone to cope with well. At work I'd keep my head down and ask Nadia what the plan is. To friends I'd say save and stay flexible. Online I'd say we need clear rules, and governments should talk to ordinary workers, not just tech bosses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my job isn't safe, even if it's old. The insurer would be able to replace the old system with an AI-built one quickly, and then they'd not need me or Nadia. I'd have maybe two years, with a loan to pay. I worry about my mum too, because she works in a care home and I don't know what she'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything but rent, food and the loan. I'd ask my mum if I could move back home for a year, which she'd say yes to. I'd start training in something hands-on and regulated, like electrical installation, since robots come three years after. And I'd stay at the insurer for as long as they'd have me, because the income matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a long exhale that doesn't end. I'm not in a panic, but I'm very aware that it's out of my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's out of your hands. What part is in your hands?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How fast I act, and how little I spend. That's the biggest lever I have. If I moved back to my mum's in the first year, I could put £700 a month on the loan and the savings. I'd hate living at home again, but I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your mum's care home job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's fifty and she's on her feet all day. If robots reach care work, she'd be one of the people it affects. In two years, she'd still be working, but I'd be worrying. I'd want to be the one in a position to help her, not the one asking.

say: I'd say it's too **fast** for anyone to cope with well.
I'd tell friends to **save** and stay flexible.
think: My job isn't safe, because the insurer could swap the old system for an AI-built one and not need **me**.
I'd have maybe two years, with a **loan** to pay.
do: Cut everything but **rent**, food and the loan.
Move back to my **mum's** for a year to put £700 a month on debt.
feel: A long **exhale** that doesn't end, aware it's out of my hands.
S2.quote: If I moved back to my mum's in the first year, I could put £700 a month on the loan and the savings.
fieldNote: He picks a clear **lever** (living at home) and states the cost to his pride.
Worry for his mother's care home job widens his fear beyond himself.
Alarm comes from a short clock and a firm that could replace the old system.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent, food and the loan
Move back to my mum's house and pay her a small rent
Start an electrical installation course in the evenings
Keep working at the insurer for as long as they have me

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years isn't long, but it's a real chance to prepare. At work I'd ask Nadia whether the firm will train us for new roles. To friends I'd say don't wait for someone to tell you. Online I'd say governments should set up retraining before the problem arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think it'll be rough but I can handle it. If I act, I could be in a role in five years that manages AI systems instead of competing with them. I like the idea of checking and testing, because I'm careful. And five years is long enough to build a proper cushion if I stay disciplined.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study part-time for a software testing or data qualification, paid for in stages. I'd save £120 a month towards a six-month cushion. I'd move to Birmingham in about two years, with a job offer. And I'd use the AI helper daily so I'm good at it before everyone else is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels workable. I'd say a bit hopeful. There's a tension in my chest that's smaller than with the first two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask Nadia, and what would you do if she said no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a day a month to learn new skills and for the firm to pay half of a qualification. If she said no, I'd study anyway in the evenings and quietly keep my CV updated. It's not rebellion, it's what a sensible person does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide when to move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When I've got a year of experience on my CV and a firm that's offered me £4,000 more. I'd also check that rent doesn't eat the difference. I'd talk it through with my mum first, because she'd miss me, and she'd give honest advice.

I'd say governments should set up **retraining** before the problem arrives.

steps.text: Start a part-time software testing qualification
Save £120 a month towards a six-month cushion
Take a Birmingham job offer paying about £4,000 more
Use the AI helper daily to become fluent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's plenty of time and we should use it well. At work I'd say the firm should plan for the long run, not the next quarter. To friends I'd say learn, save and stay curious. Online I'd say fund retraining and don't leave the young with all the debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I feel steady about it. Ten years gives me time to pay off the loan and have a proper career. I'd like to be a senior engineer or a team lead by then. The risk is that I stay comfortable and miss the moment, because I'm not a fast mover. I need to make sure I see the signs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work through a part-time master's in software engineering over about five years. I'd move to a bigger firm in Birmingham, then maybe to a role that mixes engineering with insurance knowledge. I'd save to buy a flat, with a friend if need be. And I'd help my mum with her bills if the care home work dries up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels okay. I'm calmer than I thought. The decade is a bit like a long road, and I can see the first few bends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you make sure you see the signs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check what the job adverts are asking for every six months. If AI words or new tools show up in the adverts for jobs like mine, I'd move. It's a dull little habit, but I trust habits more than moods.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does help for your mum look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Perhaps £200 a month if her hours are cut, or a small deposit for her to rent a better flat. She's never asked for money from me and she wouldn't. I'd just do it quietly. That's part of why I want a good career.

say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and the young shouldn't carry all the **debt**.
I'd tell my firm to plan for the **long run**.
think: I feel **steady**, because ten years lets me pay off the loan and build a career.
I'm not a fast mover, so I must watch for the **signs**.

Move to a bigger firm in **Birmingham**, then to a role mixing engineering and insurance.

S4.quote: I trust habits more than moods.

Move to a bigger Birmingham firm and then an insurance technology role
Save for a flat deposit with a friend
Set aside £200 a month to help my mum if her hours drop

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I can plan for five or ten years, but two doesn't give me time to build savings or switch field. What would help is retraining that doesn't need money up front, a real warning from the firm, and a loan system that pauses when you're out of work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people think a computer science degree means you're rich. I'm not. I'm renting a room, eating my mum's Sunday dinners and checking the vacancy page every Monday. I'd like people to know that a lot of us are quietly coping.

headlineQuote: I'm renting a room, eating my mum's Sunday dinners and checking the vacancy page every Monday.
portrait: Jamal is a 22-year-old computer science graduate working as a **junior developer** on an old claims system at a Leicester insurer.
He is centrist and steady, using an AI coding helper now and then and acting once things are proven.
His cushion is thin: heavy debt, **two weeks** of rent saved, and a mother who cooks him Sunday dinners.
He worries about a vanished vacancy and about few tech jobs nearby.
His plans are careful: qualifications, small savings, a possible Birmingham move with an offer.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because he'd have no time to build savings or switch field.
whatWouldHelp: Retraining without money up front, a real **warning** from the firm, and loan repayments that pause.
